speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  STATEMENT IN TENDERING RESIGNATION
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement to the house. On Friday last the Leader of the Opposition rose on a question of privilege in connection with the publication in a newspaper of two paragraphs extracted from a private letter that I wrote to a free lance writer who occasionally contributes an article to the Montreal newspaper La Patrie. Notwithstanding the fact, a well-known fact, easy to verify by those who do not know that Mr. Cinq-Mars, the author of the article in question, is only a free lance writer, the Ottawa Journal in an editorial which appeared in Saturday's edition said I wrote to the "editor" of the newspaper La Patrie.
On Friday last the Leader of the Opposition contended that if the expression "my accusers falsified the facts for their own political ends" was used in the house it would be the duty of the Speaker to call for a retraction immediately. In its Saturday editorial the Ottawa Journal supported the contention of the Leader of the Opposition in this regard. My view, well-supported, I think, that the expression would be unparliamentary only if it read "my accusers deliberately falsified the facts", was completely disregarded. I had referred
to a recent case at page 5382 of Hansard of June 26, 1956. The hon. member for Kootenay East said this:
The leader of the C.C.F. party, answering an interjection by myself, at the time he was attempting to distort the facts as he has in the past, saying that we were responsible for the breaking of the rules-
The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) rose on a point of order and asked that the expression be withdrawn. I ruled that the hon. member should indicate that:
. . . he had no intention whatever of accusing the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar of deliberately distorting the facts in this house.
On June 4 last while the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was speaking, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) rose on a question of privilege and said, as reported at page 4651 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Acadia, Mr. Speaker, has just made two remarks which are a grave offence against privilege and a falsification of the fact.
And he was not asked to withdraw.
On May 30, 1956, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) as reported at page 4462 of Hansard said the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) had deliberately deceived him. I asked the hon. member for Selkirk:
* . . because he knows it is against the rules to say that an hon. member of this house has deliberately deceived another hon. member, to take the corrective steps.
On February 16, 1956, as reported at page 1268 of Hansard, while the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) was speaking the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) rose on a question of privilege and said:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I suppose nobody should pay any attention to the ravings of the hon. gentleman opposite, but after all, when he deliberately misrepresents what I said,
I suggest that I should draw that fact to the attention of the house.
I ruled that the hon. member for Rosthern:
. . . should not indicate that the hon. member for Regina City is deliberately misrepresenting what he said.
And Mr. Speaker Macdonald made rulings also to the same effect. Some of his rulings appear in Hansard, volume I, 1952-53, at pages 271, 759 and 760. Therefore I maintain that the expression I used, namely "my accusers falsified the facts", is not an unparliamentary expression. It contains no charge of dishonesty or of insincerity. During the
5554	HOUSE OF
Mr. Speaker-Tendered Resignation debate on the unanimous report of the committee on procedure adopted at the last session, several hon. members expressed the view that as long as there were no accusations of insincerity or dishonesty, strong language should go unchecked. During this session I have taken into account the remarks that were then made.
At page 5990 of Hansard, volume VI, 1955, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had this to say on the subject:
We do not want to turn parliament into an afternoon society meeting. If we have strong opinions we want to express them. We do not want to engage in personalities as such, but if we allow our rules or Speakers' decisions to place members of parliament in the position where if they use a strong expression they have to withdraw it parliament will become nothing but a mere debating society.
After all, strong men have strong opinions. I think our trend in the last 15 or 20 years has been to reduce the standard of debate in parliament Jsy the insistence on the letter of decorum. We do not carry our ill feelings outside of the House of Commons, and the things that we say, as long as they do not impute personal wrongdoing or lack of integrity, should be permitted in the House of Commons.
Notwithstanding what has happened during the pipe-line debate and the motion of censure that followed, no hon. member had ever suggested that I should resign. I may say, however, that I intended to resign more than once during that period for the purpose of regaining my full freedom of speech both in and outside this house. I had received communications and I had an exchange of views with some of the 35 members who had voted in favour of the motion of censure on Friday, June 8 last. It appeared to me that time might bring about a situation by virtue of which it might be possible for me to carry on at least until the prorogation of this session. When paragraphs of a private letter of mine were published in a newspaper I knew I had to take immediately the course I had in mind to follow.
In public life all men have had the experience of being quoted when they spoke off the record, or of being misquoted. I realize, however, that if the accident happens to one who is occupying my position, the house to which I am responsible-and I am responsible to the house alone-may ask for an account of the incident. That was done last Friday. It appeared to me that the hon. members of the opposition exaggerated the importance of the incident and since they were accusing me of improper conduct and of having used unparliamentary language I felt that the traditional parliamentary recourse in such cases should be taken, a recourse which I think is a protection for the house and for
IMr. Speaker.]

the Chair, namely that a motion dealing with the accusations should be placed on the order paper, debated and decided. It was said in the press that my language at that point was confusing. Here is what I said, as reported at page 5514 of Hansard of June 29, 1956:
I want to tell hon. members that ever since I was appointed on November 12, 1953 my resignation has always been at the disposal of the house. If one wishes to move a motion, after 48 hours' notice, stating the reasons why and concluding that the Speaker be removed I will resign immediately.
Later, in my office, I inserted the references to the citations of Beauchesne's third edition, citations 127, 225 and 46. For the insertion of these references it has been said by the parliamentary correspondent of the Montreal Gazette, in an article appearing on the editorial page for Monday, July 2, 1956:
He is open to attack for tampering with Hansard.
All Speakers have inserted the references to the authorities interspersed with their remarks, whether in Hansard or in the Journals because, indeed, it is their duty to do so. Standing order 12 states:
In explaining a point of order or practice, he shall state the standing order or authority applicable to the case.
When I said "If one wishes to move a motion" some understood that as soon as the notice of motion appeared on the order paper I would resign. Once a motion is moved it is in the possession of the house and must be disposed of. Citation 322 of Beauchesne's third edition says:
Every matter is determined in the House of Commons upon a question put by the Speaker on a proposition submitted by a member and resolved either in the affirmative or negative as the case may be. A motion is a proposal made by one member, in accordance with certain well established rules, that the house do something or order something to be done, or express an opinion with regard to some matter or thing. The proposal is not a motion until it has been actually moved.
Now, I thought that I was entitled to have the house judge my actions. I have been in public life since 1945. My strongest critics have said that until the pipe-line debate I had acquired a good reputation as Speaker of this house. I have a family, friends and a constituency. For their sakes, as well as for my political future, I thought that I was entitled to get the judgment of the house on the incident referred to last Friday. Otherwise, notwithstanding the fact that I had admittedly a good record until the pipe-line debate and that the motion of censure arising out of the pipe-line debate was defeated by the house by a vote of 109 against 35, would it not appear, if I were to resign now without a judgment of the house, that because a newspaperman published extracts of a

private letter of mine, I have done worse than anything I might have been accused of before?
Now, last Friday the Leader of the Opposition, speaking about the above-mentioned paragraphs that were published, concluded by asking the Acting Prime Minister to dissolve the house. I do not wish my actions to be part of the many considerations which must be weighed before such a grave decision is taken. Furthermore, I am anxious to regain my full freedom of speech. I realize that the Prime Minister is away. Were I to resign today the house would have to adjourn immediately. The Senate being adjourned for three weeks, it would have to be called back in session and the presence of His Excellency the Governor General or his deputy would be required for the approval of the new Speaker.
I place now my resignation before the house to take effect at the pleasure of the house. I would wish that it be accepted as soon as possible.
This is my farewell speech. I shall always remember with pleasure my term of office as Speaker. I have enjoyed every moment of it, even the most difficult parts, because I know that deep down in their hearts members understood certainly much more perhaps than they were indicating.
In private I had conversations and exchanges of views and I know that, notwithstanding what has happened, I retain in this house the friendship of many more members than one would like perhaps to believe. I must have enjoyed every moment of it. I have never been avoidably absent since I became Speaker. I have been in this house every sitting day since November 12, 1953.
Now, I have no animosity whatever against anyone. Throughout my term of office, I assure you, I have never acted, nor have I ever been motivated, by any other interests but the best interests of the house itself. Never was I motivated by any partisan feelings; and my conscience is perfectly clear. Had it not been as clear as it is, I do not think I could have gone through all the difficulties that came my way in the past month.
Now, I thank you very much for the privilege and the honour that you have given me of serving you as Speaker of the house and I want to assure you that as long as I live I shall never forget this honour that you have given me and this kind gesture on your part. Unintentionally I might have done something wrong or I might have done something offensive to hon. members. I want to ask them-and I do say this is the last favour, if I may be deserving of a last favour-that, if I have done something offensive or anything wrong to any hon. member, an act of oblivion
Trade-British Caribbean Area will be passed. Gentlemen, thank you very much.

speechtext:
I take pleasure in announcing a trade development in the British Caribbean which will further assist Canadian exports to that area. We have now been informed that the British Caribbean countries will place apples, leaf tobacco, chemical fertilizers and calcium carbide under world open general licence effective today, July 2, 1956. This means that these products will henceforth be permitted import from Canada without restrictions. These products are of importance to many Canadian exporters. With this further liberalization, a large proportion of our exports to the area are now completely free of restriction.
Hon. members will appreciate that we have over the years maintained close and continuing consultations with British Caribbean countries and the United Kingdom with the object of developing our trade with that area to the greatest possible extent. In these circumstances this additional measure of trade

Inquiries of the Ministry liberalization is especially welcome and will serve to strengthen further the close and traditional commercial ties which exist between those countries and Canada. In 1955 Canadian exports to the area amounted to $42 million. These exports are increasing this year. With the new federation which is emerging in the British Caribbean we look forward to a further expansion of mutually advantageous trade.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 349, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. Langlois (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is largely of a technical character. Some clauses are the correction of errors which crept into the framing of the Canada Shipping Act of 1934. Other clauses bring
Canada Shipping Act
certain older provisions, which were carried' over from the Merchant Shipping Act of' 1894, into line with modern marine practice. Ocean-going vessels of modern construction, will benefit from the proposed amendment to the tonnage regulations, while operators: of small coasting vessels in our domestic trade will find it easier to comply with requirements as to certificates of those incharge of the navigation and of engines. The crews of certain commercial vessels, which at present have very little protection in the matter of safety precautions, will be accorded greater protection. The vast and ever-growing pleasure-boating public will have some protection against the foolhardly and irresponsible-minority.
Finally, our thousands of miles of coastline, including the shores of the great lakes,, will be protected against pollution by indiscriminate disposal of waste oil from ships.,
I do not intend to go into the details of the bill, but I deem it necessary at this stage to. make a brief explanation of its main features.
First, then, concerning those clauses having-to do with registry of ships. As hon. members are well aware, registration of ships is an important feature in maritime practice. The whole of part I of the Canada Shipping Act, comprising some 113 sections, is devoted to it. A ship's certificate of registry is her identity certificate, her passport in her jour-neyings to and fro in the commerce of the-world. The particulars set out in the certificate are accepted without question by government officials of foreign countries; the tonnage as shown is accepted wherever the ship may go as the basis for port charges, and the other-sundry charges which a ship must meet when she enters port. Registry is not only evidence of a ship's right to fly her national flag, but also establishes ownership title and gives the shipowner the right to invoke certain pro-, visions regarding limitation of liability.
The procedures of registration are nob. onerous, when they involve property amounting to hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions, of dollars in one vessel, but we feel they are hardly necessary in the case of very small vessels which never leave our own shores.
At present only vessels of less than 10 tons net tonnage are exempt from registry. The purpose of clause 2 of the bill is to increase this figure to 15 tons of net tonnage. On the other hand, the proposed amendment does not deprive a person of the privilege of registering a smaller vessel if he wishes to take this, trouble, in order to obtain any of the benefits, that flow from registration.

Canada Shipping Act
Clause 3 of the bill, proposing a new section of the act, may look somewhat formidable, but its purpose can be simply explained. Tonnage measurement is a vital part of registry procedure. Since most port charges are made on the net tonnage of the ship, the efforts of naval architects have always been directed to the design of ships with low net tonnage and high carrying capacity. As now provided in section 94 and in the seventh schedule, the net tonnage is arrived at by first measuring all the enclosed spaces in the ship to get the gross tonnage, then making certain deductions. One of the deductions is for the space required for the propelling power, and section 95 of the act lays down the rule governing the allowance that may be made on this account.
The United Kingdom government have already amended the British merchant shipping acts to bring this feature into line with modern construction, so that ship owners might reap a proportionate benefit in reduction of net tonnage, when modern machinery allows them to devote less space to the propelling power. They consulted us before doing so, and we undertook to take similar action in Canada at an appropriate time. If we do not, ships registered in Canada are at a disadvantage regarding tonnage, as compared with ships registered in the United Kingdom and elsewhere.
Clause 6 is designed to be of assistance to the fishing industry. In recent years it has been difficult to get fully certificated engineering personnel for fishing vessels and we have had to meet the situation by granting temporary permits in many cases.
There are quite a number of men available, who have reasonably good understanding of the duties required for certain types of engine room work, but apparently there is a shortage of men available who can pass the examination as fourth class engineers. Moreover, it does not appear necessary that the same requirements in this respect should apply to fishing vessels as to passenger or cargo vessels. Accordingly, this amendment, while maintaining the qualifications required for the chief engineer on fishing vessels, will provide for some relaxation in regard to the qualifications of additional engineering personnel, by creating a new category of watchkeeping engineer on a motor-driven fishing vessel for which modified standards will be established. Clause 8 is consequential upon clause 6 of the bill.
The department's sympathy with the difficulties experienced by the good mariners in our small domestic traders is evident in the amendments suggested in clauses 7 and 9 of the bill. Section 116 of the act sets out the grades and classes of certificates as master of

a steamship of under 150 tons in the home trade, inland waters and minor waters of Canada. Such a certificate may be obtained without prior service as mate, and does not call for the same standard of navigational and other technical knowledge as in the case of large vessels. When the existing provision was made, the vessels for which it was intended were all well under 150 tons gross. But of late years it has been found that the vessels, which are often constructed by the owner-masters themselves, without benefit of naval architectural assistance, have exceeded this critical tonnage quite considerably. We are of the opinion that this class of certificate should now be made available for vessels of up to 350 tons gross, and that holders of existing certificates should be granted the wider privilege. This will be accomplished by clause 7 of the bill.
Section 119 provides for certificates of service, which may be obtained by those seamen who may have lived their lives in small vessels on our coasts and in the St. Lawrence and who have demonstrated in a practical way their ability to command their own vessels, but who are handicapped by the lack of basic education. When the existing provision was made a time limit was included, and it was thought that the time provided would suffice to allow all interested seamen to become properly certificated. In this regard it appears that sufficient allowance was not made for the natural reluctance of the practical seaman, particularly when he is no longer young, to subject himself to any kind of examination, even the simple oral one which is all that is required in this instance. The amendment proposed in clause 9 of the bill gives the provision a continuing effect and widens its scope. It is hoped that in time, by a process of persuasion and education, all our domestic shipmasters will eventually become properly certificated under the act.
Clause 11 of the bill provides yet another concession to the small commercial vessel operator in a proposed amendment to section 128 of the act. This widens the scope of the temporary engineer's certificate which may be issued on the basis of practical training without the added requirement of technical training.
Clauses 12 to 17 of the bill have to do with licensed pilots. The first, which will permit temporary licences to be issued for a season of navigation or any other desirable period, is obvious, but hon. members may wish an explanation of the proposed amendments to sections 354, 356 and 357 of the act.
The previous wording was reasonable enough in the old days when a ship had no

communications with the shore and pilots remained on station outside a port waiting for the arrival of ships. Nowadays it is the practice for an incoming ship to radio in her expected time of arrival, and then a pilot goes out to meet her. The proposed wording is in line with modern practice.
A proposed amendment to subsection 3 of section 354 makes it an offence to act as a pilot without a licence or to employ an unlicensed pilot, in an established pilotage district. The change in the heading preceding section 354 will give this protection to pilots in all districts, whether or not the payment of pilotage dues is compulsory.
Such sanctions against the use of unlicensed pilots have long been a feature of pilotage laws in the United Kingdom, and are considered reasonable. Hon. members will understand that the proposed provisions do not affect the right of the master of a ship to do without a pilot. However, if he employs a pilot-that is, any person other than a member of his own crew-that person must hold a licence issued by the pilotage authority of the district.
Clauses 18 to 24 of the bill deal with safety measures which fall within the purview of steamship inspection. The amendments to sections 477 to 479 accord to the crews of non-self-propelled vessels and of vessels such as dredges, a certain measure of protection which they have not hitherto enjoyed, when they go more than 15 miles from land.
The amendment to subsection 3 of section 494 places sealing vessels in the same general category as fishing vessels and whaling vessels for the purposes of part VII of the act. This is important for the province of Newfoundland.
Clause 25 of the bill proposes a new part VIIA, entitled "Oil Pollution". In 1954 Canada was represented at an international conference on pollution of the sea by oil. The convention which resulted, and which is set out in clause 29 of the bill as a proposed fourteenth schedule to the act, is the first concrete attempt by the leading shipping nations of the world to stop dumping of waste oil from ships on the high seas. Certain zones of the oceans are set out where the dumping of waste oil will be prohibited. A fifty mile prohibited zone along the North American coast line will protect Canada in this regard. Provision is also made for the setting up of reception facilities at large ports where waste oil may be disposed of without contravening regulations. Hon. members will no doubt be aware of the very great concern which has been occasioned, particularly in the United

Canada Shipping Act
Kingdom and western Europe, by the destruction of sea birds and the spoiling of the beaches by oil dumped from ships, perhaps far out at sea.
The problem has not yet reached serious proportions in this country, but prevention will be easier than cure. Accordingly, the government intends to ratify the convention. The new section 4 95A is proposed so that the necessary regulations may be made to implement the convention, and also to apply similar protective measures for the waters of the great lakes which are not covered by the convention. Officials of the department have been studying the problem as it exists on the great lakes and have discussed with our American friends the possibility of their taking parallel action at the appropriate time.
The convention as presently drafted and our proposed legislation do not provide a final and complete answer to this problem. In fact, we would have preferred to see an international agreement forbidding any pollution of the sea by oil from ships. This was the first major attempt to deal with this problem on an internationally agreed basis that has shown any measure of success. As may have been expected, at the international conference widely varying points of view were presented, with the result that the final convention represents to some extent a compromise between these varying points of view. It does, however, go some distance toward meeting the objective of complete prevention which we hope can be achieved in due course.
Clause 27 also merits a full explanation. This would amend that section of the act which applies to the operation of small boats and, in particular, pleasure boats. Since the end of the war there has been a huge increase in the amount of pleasure boating in Canada; a great deal of this has taken place in the field of power boats and has, of course, been greatly accelerated by the development of the outboard motor. There are, for example, over 36,000 power boats registered in Canada on the great lakes with engines of 10 horsepower or more and we believe an even greater number of lower power.
The department has been in receipt of many representations asking it to take further action to deal with this growing problem from the point of view of public safety. It is admitted that many power boat operators are reasonable persons who are familiar with marine traffic rules, but it is also quite apparent that a great many others may be irresponsible or foolhardy or at least completely lacking in knowledge or observance of the elementary rules of marine safety and marine traffic.

Canada Shipping Act
We have attempted to deal with this problem in several ways. The minor waters navigation regulations forbid excessive speed or dangerous operation of motor boats, but they are not sufficiently comprehensive in that there are large concentrations of these boats outside the minor waters. The requirement that boats equipped with engines of 10 h.p. or more be licensed has also been a useful step but it is not enough in itself, dealing as it does with the boat and not with the operator. It is clear from our experience, from our consultation with the R.C.M.P., who are charged with enforcement of these matters, and from the representations we have received that something more must be done.
We have made extensive distribution of literature and a special pamphlet entitled "Safety at Sea", but regardless of this the problem continues to grow. We have reached the conclusion that two further steps should now be taken. The first of these is to amend this section so that it relates not only to the minor waters but to all waters of Canada. The second is to make direct use of the well proven experience in the field of motor vehicles and develop a system of licensing for operators of power boats.
The objective will be to ensure that the department has a direct contact with the boat operator and that he has in his hands some information regarding the rules of marine safety and marine traffic and some knowledge of these rules as well. The regulations for this purpose are in the formative stage at the present time and it is intended to take a gradual approach to this problem in consultation with the R.C.M.P., with various private organizations interested in boat operations and possibly local or provincial authorities.
It is not intended to create hardship for the individual who is willing to familiarize himself with the rules of marine safety and marine traffic, nor to impose any financial penalty on him in obtaining a licence, but it is intended to establish some method by which we can encourage his knowledge of this field and ensure that he does not disregard the elementary precautions which should be observed by the operators of small pleasure boats, not just in their own interest but in the interest of those around them.
This concludes the statement which I intended to make at this stage. Before resuming my seat I wish to state to the house that it is intended after second reading to move that this bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we appreciate the comprehensive remarks of the parliamentary assistant with regard to this piece of legislation, this bill to amend the Canada Shipping Act. I suppose that those of us who have a connection with the sea are more interested but I think we all appreciate that this act must be brought up to date from year to year as the shipping nations of the world modernize their fleets and plans. We understand also that in the efforts of officials and others who are connected with such plans there is a natural tendency to grab more power in order to carry out efficiently the operations of their departments. Having said that, I think we should remember that we must be constantly on guard to preserve the rights of small operators and others who must be protected from the natural plans of the bureaucrats.
This legislation comes to us from the other place where it was dealt with most extensively. We have the value of their report of their considerations in their standing committee on transport and communications. I think this is one job that has been done by the other place which indicates that there is still some worth in their operations. They considered the bill extensively, went into the details and made quite a few worth while changes.
In going through the reports I note some of those who took an active part in the consideration of this legislation. In connection with that part having to do with fishermen and the administration of shipping, an active part was taken by two hon. members of that place from the maritimes who have extensive family backgrounds connected with the sea. Then with regard to the constitutional aspects of the bill there were two constitutional lawyers of note-there may have been more -who added considerably to the discussion on this legislation.
I think it must be realized that in the consideration of this legislation those members, of the other place included more experts than we might have available here. They took their time with the legislation and except for one small matter of controversy to which I shall refer later I think they brought forth a fairly good piece of legislation.
I think it can be said that this bill divides itself into two general parts. As the parliamentary assistant pointed out, there are the routine clauses which modernize and bring: up to date in various ways the shipping act itself. This is made necessary by changing conditions in the world and the plans of other nations. It is made necessary also because of the growth of traffic on the great lakes necessitating new certifications for

mates, engineers and pilots. It is made necessary by the more extensive use of pleasure craft. All these matters have been dealt with in fairly good fashion.
I do not have anything more on that aspect of it except to say that I hope that when we get into committee we will have some expert advice and also some specific treatment of these changes which are necessary and important but which have to be appreciated from the standpoint of the small operators, the fishermen and those who might be put out of business or affected in their daily lives.
The second part of this bill has interested me the most and I think it was the cause of some controversy in the other place. It ratifies the convention on oil pollution, that is the Canadian action which was taken at the convention two years ago. This raises a most interesting constitutional problem and I do not think we should pass over it too quickly. Unfortunately I do not have the background to discuss the intricate legal points involved, but in my reading of the activities in the other place and by some quick research I am of the opinion that this is being handled in a unique way.
It is not the first time that this method has been used, but I understand that of the two general types it is the less common. In most cases, if I have my words correct, the treaties or conventions that have been signed on behalf of Canada are brought back to parliament and, through active legislation and statute, are put into force by law. But this method-and it is the one that caused comment-is to incorporate into one of our acts or statutes the exact treaty, convention and other points that are necessary for its enforcement here. I am not saying for one minute that this is wrong, because I do not know. I realize there have been parliamentary legal experts on it who have given it considerable thought, but we remember the legislation in the 1930's that dealt extensively with this problem and we remember that it was necessary to go to the privy council in 1937 to receive a final opinion on the treaty-making powers and the necessary legislative and executive action thereto.
I mention this because I hope that we shall consider it extensively in committee. It is interesting. Probably the lawyers are the ones who are more prone to indicate a knowledge of this, but we have to be careful to make certain that this is being done in the best way possible.
That is all I have to say on second reading. As I say, I appreciate the fact that our shipping act is being modernized to some extent. We have in Canada little enough
Canada Shipping Act
interest in the sea, in shipping and in our future plans, and if this action today helps in any small way to further the cause it is agreeable to me, and I am pleased to see it.
The second point that I mentioned, regarding the constitutional aspect of it, is important, and we should not forget it. It is probably the only point that has a principle involved in it; so I suppose that it is the one aspect of the bill which we should be discussing extensively here now on second reading; but I shall be interested in following it when it reaches the committee stage, and we shall watch for all these small points that may have been overlooked. We hope that by this legislation we shall have modernized and increased our shipping laws and in that way we shall be able to take our place in the competitive world in much better fashion.

Canada Shipping Act

AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution that is before the committee is one whereby it is deemed expedient to introduce ;a measure to amend the Indian Act to provide for a number of changes in connection with the administration of the act and also to prowide for a revolving fund as therein set out. I should like for a short time to deal with the Indian Act and to make certain suggestions as to its amendment which the experience of administration has, in my opinion, made necessary. In the administration of the act I believe that the first consideration should be that the rights of Indians under treaties should be maintained and guaranteed to all Indians and for all time. Indeed, when treaties were entered into, particularly so Tar as those treaties are concerned that affect
the Indians of the western plains, an agreement was made at that time by Lieutenant Governor Morris, while in the course of negotiating one or more of these treaties, in these words:
The ear of the Queen's government will always be open to hear the complaints of her Indian people, and she will deal with her servants that do not do their duty in a proper manner.
Also the general principles connected with the administration were set out by Lieutenant Governor Morris when he negotiated with the Indians at Fort Carlton. I think that was in 1876: I quote from the general principles then enunciated:
I see the Queen's councillors taking the Indians by the hand saying we are brothers, we will lift you up, we will teach you, if you will learn, the cunning of the white man. All along that road I see Indians gathering, I see gardens growing and houses building; I see them receiving money from the Queen's commissioners to purchase clothing for their children; at the same time I see them enjoying their hunting and fishing as before, I see them retaining their own mode of living with the Queen's gift, in addition.
Those were the general principles upon which these treaties were signed. Personally I knew one of the signors, one of the chiefs- namely the chief of the Mistawasis Indians- who was a boy at the time that treaty was made at Fort Carlton. I remember with what forcefulness and eloquence he pressed for that justice which was promised and relied upon the assurance that in the administration of the Indian Act the promises of 1876 would be carried out in their entirety. For the benefit of the minister I say this. I believe that in the last year or so changes have been made which have been beneficial. I refer to changes to provide for certain types of technical training, to allow for Indians to adopt mining and prospecting. I believe that the changes in this regard have been most beneficial and that the ambit of the changes already made should be materially increased and expanded in so far as vocational training is concerned. I believe that progressive programs of technical training, within the limitations of the native ability of the Indian, deserve as far as possible to be expanded and extended.
In general with regard to administration I should like to say this. I feel that, to too great an extent, there has been a desire on the part of the administration to expand the powers of the minister. When this bill is introduced, I hope there will be no changes to increase his power at the expense of the governor in council. I have seen a draft of the sections of the bill which were submitted to the Indian representatives who met some months ago. If some of those sections are to be adopted, I say that indeed the power of the minister will be extended and that

556S
the centralization of authority in the minister will result in detrimental effects in so far as the administration of Indian affairs is concerned. Instead of centralizing power in the minister I believe that there should be more and more an expansion of the rights of Indians to their own self-government. One of the things that might be achieved in that connection is to give more Indians an opportunity to be installed in administrative positions not only in the field in the reserves but in the administration of the department here in Ottawa. While saying that, I also say that if changes are ever made whereby the minister receives further powers, I feel that provision should be made in the act to allow for appeals to the courts against administrative orders which affect the individual rights of Indians themselves. In other words, where the minister acts in a manner, administratively speaking, that has the result of determining the rights of an individual, or of a band, his decision in that regard should be subject to an appeal to the courts to the end that no one in this day and age have the right to determine the rights and privileges of peoples of other races without those persons having an appeal to the courts. All over the world coloured races are demanding that they shall no longer be subservient to the white races. In our country, the major subject of complaint on the part of Indians is that they are placed in an inferior position. There are 150,000 of them in this country, and 2,500 of them served during the past war, most of them voluntarily. Education is coming to them in larger measure though not in a sufficient way having regard to the potentialities of those people. Certainly, they have the right to demand that they shall not be subject to the ipse dixit of the minister, and their rights determined without having the right to appeal to the courts.
I mention that because Indians object very strongly to being placed in a position of being not second-class citizens but second-class people, to whom the courts of law in large measure against arbitrary and unjust actions on the part of the administrators are not open. In that connection, I should like some provision made whereby Indians would have an assured right of appeal against any orders or convictions made against them by the summary courts of criminal jurisdiction in our country. I think of an example that arose the other day. An Indian becomes intoxicated and pleads guilty to the charge. There is no reason whatever why, under those circumstances, a person should receive a jail sentence for a first offence. He is sentenced to two months in jail. He is a married man living on the reserve. He is sent away to
Indian Act
serve his term at a time when he is just about to commence upon his farming operations. I believe when sentences of imprisonment for petty offences such as that are pronounced against Indians the department should see to it that there is an appeal in order to assure a reasonable equality of sentences and thereby deny any perversion of justice.
In that connection, I point out another subject of complaint. When a treaty Indian commits an offence he is subject to a summary conviction trial before a justice of the peace appointed by the department of Indian affairs. However honourable such persons may be, none the less they have not that freedom from external influence which our courts should have and to which every Canadian, whether white or Indian, should be entitled. In other words, I believe that the section of the act that today makes possible the appointment of justices of the peace by the department of Indian affairs, or by the governor in council, should be removed, and Indians should be tried in the ordinary courts before magistrates who have the necessary ability and also the experience to assure that inequality and inequity in the present system would be reasonably removed. After all, when an Indian serves a term in jail the effect on his health is detrimental; it stays with him sometimes for years. A jail sentence of two months should not be imposed upon Indians for the simple offence of being, intoxicated.
I believe, too, that in so far as these minor offences are concerned, such as are provided for in the Indian Act, a fine should be sufficient. Provision might well be made in the Indian Act so that instead of there being a default, except in a limited number of cases, the Indian would be able to make payment of his fine in instalments to the end that imprisonment and its stigma would not be impressed upon him.
Now, sir, having said that, I feel that the-resolution in question, which constitutes apparently in part a series of amendments based on the experience of the last few years, is premature, and that before the Indians in Canada can properly receive that consideration to which they should be entitled the law should be brought up to date and the Indian Act made an instrument of justice for the Indians of our country rather than in some-cases, as it is, an agency of tyranny in its present form. I believe the first thing that should be done is to appoint a royal commission which would meet in all parts of Canada at appointed times and places so that the-Indian's point of view might be placed before the Canadian people as a whole rather than through the narrow conduit pipe of the

Indian Act
administrative services within the department itself. There are tremendous problems at stake in the administration of the Indian. These problems will never be met by a piecemeal haphazard amendment of the act from time to time. They can only be met by viewing the problem in the national sense through the medium of a royal commission of men and women who have some knowledge of Indian affairs so that recommendations may be made for the amendment of the act which will remove many of the inequalities and injustices of the present.
We have royal commissions appointed on everything else. Why not a royal commission on Indian affairs? If a royal commission were appointed, Indians would feel free to appear through representatives from each of their bands to place before that commission their demands, their requirements and their suggestions for the improvement of the act. A number of commissions have sat within the last three years on the question of band membership. Those commissions were one-man commissions. They sat in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and in Ontario in one or two cases. They consisted of a commissioner whose authority it was to hear evidence regarding the challenged rights of certain persons on the reserves to be considered as Indians. I am not going into the particulars of the number of sittings that took place but there were 17 of these commissions and they sat in 1954.
Under the provisions of the Indian Act as It now stands, these commissions did not examine the questions with which they were charged and had the responsibility to undertake by anything approaching the laws of evidence. They proceeded on the basis of the sheerest hearsay in many cases. Their purpose was to ascertain whether or not certain individuals on the reserves whose status was challenged were or were not Indians. I took no part personally in any one of these but I was present when two of the commissioners sat, and what passed as evidence was a denial of every principle that should be in effect if the rights of individuals are to be protected. It is true there was a right to appeal for a review by the minister and also by a district or county court judge, as the *case might be, but here was the kind of evidence I heard.

speechtext:
The minister is right; I am speaking without the act before me. This is an example of the kind of evidence that was given: Someone would turn up who was called to give evidence concerning party A who was challenged as not being an Indian.

He might say, "My grandmother told me when I was a boy that A's grandfather was a white man". Well, Mr. Chairman, that type of hearsay evidence could not but arouse feelings of intense antagonism among the Indian tribes on reservations where the commissions sat. The commissions had the power by way of evidence to determine whether A, B or C as the case might be was indeed an Indian within the meaning of the act. I know of nothing that has taken place on Indian reservations or among Indians within the last 25 or 30 years that aroused such intense feelings of antagonism and animosity as between band presidents.
The minister might say, "Well, the Indians asked for this." It is indeed one of the few things the Indians asked for that they ever got, but it is one of those things that naturally provide a short-cut in the determination as to whether or not a person is indeed an Indian; but in the manner in which it was administered under the law passed by this house it had the effect of creating feelings of antipathy, arousing false motives on the part of those who would benefit by having reduced the number of people on a reserve entitled to be called Indians. There were jealousies, ancient antipathies and fears. There were all the motives that cause men to act differently than normal men and women. All these things brought about a state of disagreement and ill-feeling that should never have been permitted to take place.
Even at this late date I am asking the minister whether it would not be in the interests of amity and good spirit on these reservations if whatever was done by these commissions should be entirely obliterated. Whatever the findings were-whether or not the findings were correct as regards certain individuals being entitled to be considered as members of the band-the manner in which the commissioners sat and the sittings of the commissions themselves brought about a situation that was a negation of the kind of tranquility that should be established and fostered on reserves, and brought about a feeling of hostility that will only be obliterated in possibly one or more generations. I say that because I believe even now the minister should realize the situation has arisen everywhere in this country and should endeavour as far as possible to remove the adverse effects which the commission system brought into being. After all, there are three, four or five hon. members of this house-my friend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is one and I am another- who have been honoured by appointment as chiefs of Indian tribes. The Indians come to us and ask us to present their views before parliament. They have no direct representation. As a matter of fact, I have often thought

that the only way in which our 150,000 Indian people in Canada who have no representation in parliament could receive representation would be through the appointment to the Senate of one or more of their outstanding leaders to the end that their problems will receive that consideration which only direct representation in parliament, either in the Senate or in the House of Commons, will permit.
I therefore sum up the views I have endeavoured to place before the committee. In the first place, a royal commission should be appointed. Second, the powers of the minister which permit of the arbitrary exercise of rights determining individual privileges and rights on reservations should be subject to an appeal to the courts. If the orders that are made by the minister determining the rights of individuals are worth while and have a sound basis, there should be no fear of having the courts review them when and if any Indian feels he is aggrieved thereby.
Third, the provisions concerning the appointment of a justice of the peace to try infractions under the Indian Act should be removed from the statutes and those Indians should be permitted trial before regular magistrates in the several provinces in this country. Surely we do not have to have a system that denies one group of people in this country, the Indian population, the right to be tried for summary conviction before the same courts that try all the other people in Canada. The Indians should not be restricted to trial before justices of the peace who indirectly owe their *appointments to the Indian department. We should have reached the stage in our development where no judicial officer should directly or indirectly find himself in the position where he has to act both as judge and as interested party.
Fourth, I suggest that the provisions for commissions to investigate the rights of Indians to be on reserves and be considered as Indians should be entirely obliterated and the band list as determined by the Indian reservation residents themselves should be accepted as the basis for future determination as to qualifications for Indians after this date.
These are but three or four suggestions which I have to offer. I couple them with the need for a pronounced expansion in the vocational training of Indians. They have done amazingly well under the plans brought into being by the minister in connection with prospecting for minerals. They have caught on to this and many of them are receiving large wages, far beyond what they could have ever hoped for in other activities. They have a natural aptitude for the outdoors and
Indian Act
a natural ability to do those things in the outdoors which a prospector must do.
Then what about provisions to raise the standards of Indians on the reservations? I suggest that there should be provision in the act for a trained welfare worker on every reserve to the end that residents on the reserve would receive the benefit of instructions which only a person such as that could give, thereby bringing about improved economic conditions.
From that item arises one other, the amounts furnished today to indigent Indians for upkeep, food and relief assistance. According to the information I have this allowance is at the starvation level of some $7.75 per month. This is something which should be altered. Today Indians are removed from the time when they could provide their livelihood by hunting and fishing. The white man has made that almost impossible and for that reason indigent Indians and those unable to take care of themselves should be assured of at least a reasonable living, something that is not possible under the allowances paid today.
The objective of the Indian department should be a wider expansion of local selfgovernment on the reserves. Give to the chiefs and their councillors allowances in keeping with their responsibilities. I have not the latest figures, but I know of no change in that regard, and I understand that the chief today receives $25 a year while the councillors receive $15 a year each.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one of those in this country who point with such pride to our economic prosperity, it is with a feeling of some embarrassment that I find it necessary to rise and make a plea for Canada's most impoverished citizens. At the outset I should like to say that I support the proposed legislation with one or two reservations which I shall make known later. When we are enjoying such prosperity in this country I feel it is rather embarrassing that we have to admit that we have approximately 150,000 people who have been and still are being relegated to a role of unimportance within the economy of the country. It is embarrassing to admit that living conditions such as we find on Indian reserves across this country do exist. We have to admit also that we are still unprepared to accept these people as anything but second-class citizens.
I had hoped for the last three years that there would be a new approach to the whole Indian problem. I had hopes that the present minister would go to great lengths to revise and improve the existing Indian Act. Certainly he knows the problem because he has admitted it on many occasions. A prime example of that admission will be found in the Indian News of January of this year. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is pointing out the problem that exists, and he goes on to say:
-there are only two ways in which we can carry on in this country in the future. One way is by the Indians living off in a corner by themselves and having as little to do with the rest of us as possible, and the other is by our getting together and working together and living together as brothers, and as equals, to make this a better country for all of us.
That is a most worthy admission on the part of the minister. When the minister was speaking to the delegation of Indian representatives here in Ottawa he said that something should be done about the conditions which exist. He went on to discuss the purpose of the conference at which changes in the Indian Act were to be considered, and he continued:
Now nothing we are going to suggest, nothing I am going to put before you, is different from the principles of the old act.
I think that was most unfortunate.

speechtext: As I said at the beginning, if we are not to have a new act or a new approach to the old act, then we are left with no choice but to support the legislation before us with one or two reservations. It was unfortunate the other day that the minister was reluctant to discuss the administrative changes referred to in the first part of the resolution.

That is the very point I am trying to make. While I am in favour of the proposal covered by this resolution, I think its success or failure hinges entirely upon the administrative changes which we presume the minister is going to propose. To suggest that the increase that is mentioned is going in any way to benefit the Indians without any change in the administration is, I feel, a complete delusion. I hope that when the bill is at the proper stage we shall have some indication of what that change in administration is going to be.
I was rather amazed when I tried to find out on what basic information this house is asked to subscribe something in the neighbourhood of one million dollars to increase loans to Indians under the act. Why are we being asked to do that? Apparently we are unable to find out very much authentic information through the questions that have been asked in this house, so we must try to make up our own minds as to the necessity for this increase. Certainly if we believe some of the stories we read in the press and hear over the radio as to what conditions are regarding our Indians generally, we have no alternative but to believe that conditions are not what they should be. I should like to read one or two excerpts from some of the press clippings from local newspapers that have appeared over the past month or two. According to one, Mr. Gordon Robertson, commissioner of the territories, said on Friday, May 4, before the royal commission on broadcasting:
The fur trade was the most depressed industry in Canada and the average annual income of the natives was less than $800.
The other day the hon. member for Mackenzie River mentioned the figure of $400. Again, an item appeared in my own constituency paper of January, as follows:
Needy Indian families on the Fishing lake reserve, southeast of here, are more warmly dressed as the result of an appeal for clothing and

deer skins made by Corporal Gordon Crawford of the local R.C.M.P. detachment.
He requested that local people bring old *clothing and deer skins to a central depot ior distribution. Again, we have a report of April 11, as follows:
Federal officials have begun an investigation of living conditions of 400 Indians at the Roseau river reservation about 60 miles south of Winnipeg.
An Indian affairs branch official said that the investigation followed recent Winnipeg reports that the Indians are living in three houses and 17 log cabins there.
It goes on to point out the very serious conditions that exist. Then possibly one of the most shocking items appeared in the Star-Phoenix a month or so ago, when an Indian was arraigned in court on a very serious charge. The judge in that case, Mr. Justice G. E. Taylor, took a grave view of the conditions under which Indians of the Saulteaux reserve, north of Cochin, are living. He said:
It is shocking indeed to find that such conditions can continue to exist anywhere in Canada.
J. N. Conroy, Q.C., then described the conditions that exist:
Mr. Conroy described their reserve as an area of "hills, sand and stones, not capable of cultivation". Its people, he said, "can neither read or write. They have no schools. They know nothing of religion, or the customs or morals of civilization.
"They are a race apart-" . . .
Whilst I have said I am in favour of this increase, I should like something more than newspaper reports as a justification for parliament passing this request that the minister has placed before it. So, because of that interest and because of my curiosity, I asked for certain returns, and from those returns I hoped to get a clear picture of the need for this increase. About a month ago I asked what the cash income was, thinking that possibly if I could get some answer as to the cash income of Indians across this country, it would give some indication of the economic condition in which they find themselves. I asked for the cash income each year since 1951 from the sale of grain, livestock and other products. The answer I got from the department was:
There are no official records kept of the total income of Indians. Statistics are, however, maintained for reserves on which the "permission to sell" section of the act is invoked with respect to farm produce. These figures would not necessarily be an accurate reflection of the total income of the Indians concerned.
I thought that was rather strange, because we are able to find out the income of every other group in this country.

Would the hon. member mind if I interrupted him? I had meant- and I apologize to him-to say a word to him about the answer filed to that question.

I did not wish him to think there was any desire not to give information. After considering as much information as we had available in my department, I felt it would be entirely misleading to give it.
There was another objection too. With these Indians who are given permission to sell certain things-permission is still required under the act, and I rather regret to say it is-their number is so small that if you gave it for individual reservations you would be almost disclosing the affairs of individual Indians in a way that I do not think we would do for other people in the community. But I think if the hon. gentleman wanted to get some kind of estimate such as the bureau of statistics makes, it might be possible to get something of that sort that would be sufficiently generalized so as not to disclose people's private affairs and so as to give a fairly reasonable picture, but my department does not have statistics of that sort.

speechtext:
So I undertook to ask a few questions relevant to that, because I am very much concerned about this question of supervision. I am not an expert on Indians, although I have lived near them all my life, but I know they must have supervision. After all, you do not send out even skilled workers without supervision of some kind, somebody to see that the plan is carried out. It is unfortunate, in my estimation, that the department expects these people, who are still in many cases very primitive, to go out and attempt to do the kind of job that is going to make their operation an economic possibility. So I asked a question relevant to supervision. I asked:
How many persons are presently employed as farm instructors by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Indian affairs branch?
These farm instructors are the people who are going to make or break the scheme the minister envisages in this section. The answer was:
The Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration does not employ farm instructors as such. In areas where the chief occupation of the Indian population is agriculture.

Indian Act
farming instruction is given by Indian agency assistants who also perform administrative and other functions.
Then I asked how many part-time instructors there were. There was no answer to that. Then I asked:
On what reservations are these instructors presently engaged?
There was no answer to that. Nor was there any answer to the question:
What salary do these farm instructors receive?
It was very evasive from start to finish. I took the little bulletin that is put out by the department regarding the census of Indians, and I found a very amazing revelation. There are 100 Indian agency assistants looking after 151,558 Indians. That is one Indian agency instructor for every 1,500 Indians. There are 608 bands, 87 superintendents, and so on, or one superintendent for every seven bands.
The point I am trying to make is that I feel that if this money is going to be used to the best advantage when there is very close the best advantage when there is very close administration on the reserves. Two years ago I drew the attention of the minister to a particular situation, and I want to mention it now because it has a very great bearing on this matter. I find from a return that the reservation I have in mind was in receipt of some $3,900 by way of a loan out of the original amount of $350,000.
I should like to ask this question. What benefit did these Indians actually get from that loan? I have been unable to get any information at all in that regard. However, I should like to read an excerpt from a letter written to me two months ago, and the part I wish to read has to do with conditions existing on this reserve in spite of the loan they received. A man who lives near the reserve wrote me and this is what he had to say:
I think this has been the worst time we have had with the Indians coming to the house to get warm on their way to the reserve. I keep a diary and on looking it over I find this. On the last four days we have had no less than 30 Indians . . .
These Indians came in there to try to get warm around the stove. Then he went on to say that he saw the Indian agent and the Indian agent shrugged his shoulders and said, "Throw them out." That is the kind of situation that exists on that reserve. Therefore I ask this further question relative to that condition. On that reserve there are 183 Indians and they have 348 acres of cultivated land. There you have 183 Indians trying to eke out an existence on 348 acres of land, without any supervision whatsoever.

The minister challenged my statement two years ago when I said there was no supervision on that reserve. I received a return from him pointing out that the Indian agent, had visited the reserve three times during the-summer. The fact of the matter is, as appears from the return that I received, that the-Indian agent visited the reserve in April before seeding. Then he came back early in August before harvest and came back again in November. He always came when there was actually no need for him to come. He came there before the crop had been sowed. He came back before it was harvested, and he came back after it was harvested.
Here is a situation where we have people trying to exist on less than two acres of cultivated land each, and it is not good enough. We go to great lengths to provide money for the Colombo plan for economic aid.
I feel that we in this country need a Colombo plan for our own Indians. If we are going to talk about economic aid in other parts of the world, I think we should investigate the proposition of establishing a Colombo plan with respect to our own Indians here at home.
I referred to our Indians as being second class citizens. In my area of the country a great many farmers who have land to be cleared and broken go to an operator and say they will give him the first crop clear if he will clear the trees off the land, break it and sow it at his own expense, and there are many takers. In some cases, if it costs $40 or $50 an acre to clear it, they will take the first crop and half of the second crop. But what happens on the Indian reserve when there is land to be broken? The officials of the department solicit farmers from the surrounding areas to come and bid on clearing and breaking the land, and you give them three-quarters of the crop for five years for doing it. I do not think that is giving the Indian very much of a break.
Then I should like to refer to something that I understand by the grapevine is going to take place, and I hope this is not true. I referred to this reserve where there are 183 Indians trying to operate 348 cultivated acres. They also have 1,500 acres of leased land. I know the land very well. It is on the shore of a lake and is mostly rock and trees.

speechtext:
Yes, it is part of the reserve. I understand by the grapevine that the department is going to take 100 head of heifers, breeding stock, to the reserve this spring.

I hope that is not true, because these people have no haying machinery whatsoever. They have no facilities to look after such a herd of cattle, and they will end up without any cattle or anything else. All they will have will be the companionship of some of the cows next winter. I hope the minister will advise me as to the truth of that story.
In this very informative little magazine I also read something about housing conditions on reserves. I was rather amused at the story, because the first thing I read was that hammers and saws on almost every reserve in Canada were singing a song of better housing. It sounds very interesting when you read it, but when you investigate the proposition what do you find? I am just going to take two provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I find that in Saskatchewan we have 67 Indian reservations and last year there were 62 new homes built, or something less than one home per reservation. There are 18,750 Indians on the 67 reserves, so that means one new house for each 300 Indians. In Alberta there are 47 reserves and there were 130 houses built or 2-7 houses per reserve, with about 300 Indians on each reserve.
I come back to the first point I made about supervision. We need, not only more but better Indian agents. I am sure the minister is a good enough administrator to realize that changes are necessary in that regard if we are going to have better conditions among our Indians. It is going to cost more money, and I think the people of Canada will be prepared to grant more money for this worthy cause. In my opinion we in this country stand condemned of the greatest crime in our history so far as our treatment of our Indians is concerned. I think it is time that our Indian policy was established on the principle that the Canadian Indian is a respectable individual. That is the only policy the government has not tried up to this time, and that is why we have failed so completely and miserably to even come close to finding a solution to the problem.
We are placing a great deal of emphasis on education, but I should like to say that only when we make a concerted attack at the root of the problem are we going to make any progress in education. First of all we must establish a decent economic existence for these impoverished people before we talk about interesting them in education. However, adequate educational facilities must be provided in conjunction with such a program.
I said something about the minister being a good administrator, and I hope he will prove to be a good administrator in future so far as Indian affairs are concerned. Certainly
Indian Act
if we take as our yardstick the progress in Indian welfare that has been made to date I doubt whether among the 19 members of the cabinet a worse administrator could have been found. I hope the minister will de something to better conditions as we find them. I should like to ask the minister this question. We are stuck with this Indian problem, and nobody knows it better than he does. The Indian, by the minister's own admission, is not a dying race by any stretch of the imagination; he is increasing.
We must face this problem. I should like to see the minister take one of these reserves in western Canada and set it up as an experimental station in order to see what can be done to give these people a decent economic existence. I think he is going to be obliged to abandon many of these reserves. The Indians themselves asked for land which was not suitable for agriculture. They asked for land that was situated near lakes where they could fish, but there is no longer fish in the lakes. I should therefore like to see the minister take one of these reserves that has possibilities, set it up under proper supervision as an experimental station, and see what can be done. Certainly it is going to cost money, but I think it will be worth it. Otherwise, we shall be obliged to abandon completely the reserves we have because these people are increasing in numbers and are becoming more impoverished as time goes on.
I should like to see the administration divided between the province, as much as possible, and the central government. When you are dealing with people scattered through the ten provinces, local conditions and provincial conditions are different. I think it would be to the advantage of all concerned if the administration of this problem were shared between the province, as much as possible, and the federal authority. I feel that the Indian problem will not solve itself. We made the problem, and we must accept, the major responsibility for solving it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in all I say today I want the minister and every other member in the chamber to realize that I fully appreciate the fact that in dealing with the Indian problem you are dealing with a major problem. It is a matter about which it is extremely easy to find fault but. exceedingly difficult to prescribe a remedy and produce results. I have spent my life within two miles of the Blood Indian reservation. The Blood Indian reservation is one of the finest reservations in Canada, and the Blood Indians are one of the finest tribes;

Indian Act
in Canada, if not the finest. I say that without reservation, and not because they happen to be in my constituency.
I have greatly appreciated what has been said by the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. Everything those hon. members said was true, valuable and pertinent; and everything those two said must be met head on, with no sidestepping whatsoever, because they are picturing facts just as they are. The speech given the other night by the hon. member for Mackenzie River was again an exceedingly valuable one that must be met head on.
Ever since we started dealing with Indians, or rather ever since our forefathers did so, I think there has been a failure to realize a most important fact, namely that the Indian population of the Dominion of Canada is potentially a magnificent asset or a dreadful liability. Whether it is going to become a magnificent asset or a formidable responsibility rests upon us who are charged with the responsibility of administering the act under which the Indians are supposed to try to live. There is no doubt that our Indian population-and I say this as a result of my observations of the Indians-as far as I have met them-consists of splendid men and splendid women in potentiality. If they are given a chance such as that which we demand for our own children and our fellows, they will measure up in a highly commendable way.
Up to the present time, as I have seen ourselves in action in respect of Indians-and while I was sitting in the committee on the Indian Act I kept thinking of this over and over again-the first thing we always think about when we think about Indians is how to save money. We try to put the dollar sign on every single thing we think and say about Indians when as a matter of fact the first -thing we ought to be thinking about is Indians, how to make them the great people the Creator intended they should be, and the magnificent people they were before the white man came to this country. Let the dollar sign take care of itself. We have been altogether too niggardly in the past. We should be treating our Indian population as .a sort of big business in Canada.
It is easy for us to hear men like the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, whom I Honour because of his contribution this afternoon and the careful study he has devoted to this problem-it is easy to hear him speak about the Indians consisting of 150,000 or more, but it is extremely difficult for us to realize what 150,000 people would look like if you- had them all close together
[Mr. Blackmore.I
where you could get a good look at them; how much it would take to feed, clothe, shelter and educate them; and how many resources and what kind of resources they would require to have access to if they were to supply these things themselves. I refer to the feeding, clothing, sheltering and educating.
With us it is largely a matter of money, as I have already indicated. I know that we are faced with serious financial difficulties in this nation, but we are not faced with any difficulties in connection with producing food, clothing, shelter, the means of educating or of giving hospitalization. We are not faced with that problem at all. Let us not forget that fact for one minute. If we are worried about money, it is likely to be our own fault. The Indians cannot do a thing about that money question. They are helpless. Today they can do very little about producing, because in that respect they are likewise largely helpless.
Having said these things, I want the minister not to feel that I am finding fault with the way in which he is administering the Indian department. I believe the minister has approached this problem with just as great sincerity, resourcefulness and initiative as did the present Minister of Finance; and I doubt that the country ever had a finer minister in charge of Indian problems than the present Minister of Finance.
