There are several principles which I think must be laid down. I found when I was on the Indian Act committee

there were a good many who did not agree with me; but after the thinking I have done, which may not be of the very highest type, and after the experience I have had with Indians-and I have been on plenty of reservations-I have come to the conclusion that the things I am going to lay down are principles which are essential in dealing with the Indian problem.
I would say the first thing, Mr. Speaker-[DOT] and I believe the minister agrees with all these things; I hope he will not think there is any criticism implied-we must do is to keep the reservation inviolate. Every reservation in this Dominion of Canada must be kept at least as good as it is now, and retained that way for generations yet to come. It must be improved if possible and wherever possible, but it must not be allowed to deteriorate.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort spoke of the increase in the population. It is true the Indians are increasing in numbers; we want them to do so. We are providing them with family allowances and old age pensions to encourage them to do so. We should be providing them with greater family allowances and old age pensions to encourage them to do so, because as far as I know Indians will be loyal and true to this nation, which is a great deal more than you can say about a whole lot of the questionable characters we have been dragging into this country in droves in the last 15 or 20 years, people who would rather cut our throats than say hello to us, only they do it in a sneaking underhand way, behind the curtain or in the dark. Therefore I say we want the Indian population to increase. They are great people.
Now, then, if the Indian population increases-and it is increasing on the reservation in my constituency, the Blood Indian reservation-why have we not added to the acreage in that reservation in conformity with the increase in the population? Why did we make the reservation in the beginning the size it was then? Had the size of the reservation any relation whatsoever to the number of Indians which it was contemplated would be expected to maintain themselves on the reservation? If not, then certainly it was an oversight. Should we not in a very broad way fit the size of a reservation to the population of the Indians who are required to live on that reservation? Wherever it is found that the size of a reservation is not in conformity with the number of Indians who have to keep themselves on that reservation we had better look into the matter with the determination to make the reservation larger or more productive. I say that is the first great principle.
We should increase the productivity of the reservation by such things as wood lots, fish 67509-354
Indian Act
ponds, pasture lands and game. A lot of people I have talked to gasped when I talked about a thing like that. Well, how in the name of common sense do you suppose an Indian gets his wood with which to keep himself warm? Seventy-five years ago there was wood all over the place and in every water course, where he could help himself and get all the wood he wanted; there were ponies running all over the range that he could use. Well, today he cannot find any place where he can go and get a bit of firewood for his home without being warned off by a white holder of the property.
Why have we not looked into the matter of planting wood lots and maintaining them where an Indian on the reservation has not a wood lot and where wood is at a premium? How do you think Indians can afford to buy coal the way we can? Where are they going to get the money to pay for the coal? For instance, in my own riding time and again I have seen the Indians struggling along. When I think of how much it costs my family for coal to keep ourselves warm and what we have to spend on food and clothing and every other thing that we need to live, I often say to my wife I do not see how on earth the Indians live at all.
I do not wish to elaborate or take too much time on the matters I have mentioned, but they are matters that ought to be taken care of. The Indians used to be able to go fishing all over the place 75 years ago. When they signed the treaties in the west in 1877 they could fish anywhere; they could take prairie chicken and other game birds anywhere, and, as I have said, they could get firewood anywhere. They could pick fruit in abundance, on every hillside, and a little while before that there were buffalo in abundance, and deer. There was a wide variety of game, and there were rabbits on pretty nearly every reservation. You can go across the average reservation today almost without seeing a sign of any of these things. What are the Indians living on?
I would like to elaborate on the remarks of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. It would be a very fine thing for the minister if he could possibly select a reservation somewhere, if he feels they are satisfactory, and then take the number of white men that would correspond to the number of Indians that he would expect could make a living there, put the white men there and see if they could live where Indians are trying to live, with no more access to productive capacity than the Indians have.
In the reservation in my constituency there is plenty of room for wood lots and plenty of room for fish ponds. Until the St. Mary

Indian Act
dam was built I do not believe we ever thought of increasing the number of fish in the streams in which the Indians used to fish. We took no steps so far as I know. I hope the minister is doing that, and I am sure he will do it after I get through talking. We took no steps to increase their pasture facilities. Wherever I go the white men around are just simply straining to get in on the Indian reservations and rent their lands for pasture. It is good that they do, because in many instances the Indians have not the cattle to pasture on the land. But the main thing is that they never take any thought of improving the pasturing on their lands. Something should be done to renew the pasture.

As I said a moment ago there is a great deal of land which we are taking over and finding unsuitable for farming. I do not see one valid reason why we should not build pastures, as the Minister of Agriculture has done under the P.F.R.A., in which we could allow the Indians to participate. There is another very important matter. I do not wish to do any harm to any hon. member who served with me on the committee examining the Indian Act, but during our sittings there seemed to be a feeling that what we wanted to do was to get the Indians off the reserves, wash our hands of them and dust our trousers and say, "That's that''. As I said when I first spoke, we must treat these reservations, shall I say, as sanctuaries to which the Indians can return.
If we were to take the Indian boys and girls and give them the finest education and training that we might give to white youth and they were to go into ordinary society, they would be under a tremendous disadvantage in the average community purely because of personal characteristics. Can you imagine how popular an Indian doctor would be? Can you imagine what success an Indian dentist or an Indian school teacher or lawyer would have? I know there are some who succeed but when you think of how many white people fail, with all their advantages, you would not be surprised to find that a great many of these people would fail, not because they were incompetent in their profession but simply because the white people would not want to go to an Indian.

Well, I have had a certain amount of experience in these matters, and I am certainly not hurting the Indian; I am

boosting him up and my hon. friend should be glad of that. He puts himself up as a great defender of Indians and an advocate of their welfare, but I want this to be understood. As far as I can see, if you trained the average Indian to the very highest degree he would still be under a serious disadvantage in open competition with white people among whom he hoped to dwell. In an age when unemployment is so common and jobs are so hard to get we must not imagine that just because we train these Indian boys and girls they are going to be successful. Many an Indian who had fine personal qualifications himself might have a child who would not have those qualifications. This happens among white people with great frequency. If the father of that child should have left the reserve and established himself independently, his children who did not inherit the qualifications they would need in order to live off a reserve would have to be able to go back in time of need. I think this is a matter that must not be disregarded.
For the reason I have just given I think we have to safeguard the band membership of Indians. I do not think we can afford to leave it entirely to the bands of Indians to determine whether Indians are going to be on reserves. If people have Indian blood in their veins, even if it is only one-twelfth or one-sixteenth, they may be parents of children who will have all the characteristics of full-blooded Indians. These children will likely have to go back to a reservation and claim the right of the reservation to which they should belong. I think provision must be made for this sort of case looking to the future, if we are to approach this problem in a realistic way with a long range view.
Certain things have been said by various men and certain things have been said by the minister which have caused the Indians much concern. The Indians fear he wants to get them off the reservations. For instance, the minister has used the expression "integrating the Indian with the white population". Throughout his life the Indian has been taught to suspect everything the double-tongued white man said; therefore when the double-tongued white man says "integrate the Indian with the white population" the Indian concludes that means taking him off the reserve, putting him in open competition with the white man and taking away the treaty privileges his forefathers were promised.
As far as integration is concerned I think it must be as a result of self motivation on the part of the Indians; it must be by teaching the boys and girls that they can succeed very well off the reserves.

No pressure must be put. on them in any way, shape or form. When; they integrate a good many of them will intermarry. I know of a good many combinations which are apparently quite successful, where Indians and white people have married. If they do that of their own free will and choice it is fine, and I believe they will eventually become white people; but let us have the instigation and pressure coma from them and not from us.
There is another matter to which I wish to devote some attention and that is the preservation of the native religion, history and culture. The Indians have a great, culture, a great history and a great religion.-The ancestors of our Indians created those magnificent pieces of architecture we find down in Central America. It was not second rate citizens who produced those great works, and no doubt they were created by people of the same blood and with the same ability as our Indians. The Indians have a great history and they should know about it, because it will inspire them. They had a great religion, or they would not have produced those great works; and they should know about it. Whether or not they choose to follow their native religion ought to be a matter of their personal choice, but I believe they should know about all these things.
There is another matter which I think deserves some attention, and that is the matter of choosing the band council. Formerly in all the reservations and among all the bands the Indians who led the bands were people who had a hereditary right to do so, and the Indians were led by those who came from great families. We are now-trying to introduce on many of the reservations the idea that the Indians should elect their representatives rather than select those whose heredity would qualify them for the position.
That poses a difficult problem, as the minister knows only too well, but my judgment is that the Indians themselves should be the judges as to whether they will choose as their band council those hereditary leaders or whether they will choose others whom they may consider better fitted for the task. Great care ought to be exercised in this matter.
Having visited the Indian reserve in my own constituency the minister will remember how far it is from one end of that reserve to the other. Just imagine-the minister will get the picture immediately-a meeting called just north of Cardston at which the Indians are going to elect a band council. How many of the Indians who dwell down

Indian Act
near Lethbridge are going to be able to attend that meeting? How many of them are going to be able to afford it? There will also be many Indians to the north and west who will be unable to attend the meeting, and the result will be that a great percentage of the Indians will not be able to attend. Who will be the people who will select members for the council? It will be a little group of Indians who live within three or four miles of the area just north of Cardston. That is the kind of thing which needs to be given much thought in managing Indians.
It was either the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort or the hon. member for Prince Albert who suggested that the Indians believed that if they got the franchise they would have to give up their treaty rights. The Indians in my constituency have that idea. They are fearful that if they vote they will disqualify themselves from getting their treaty rights. That shows there should be no relationship between an Indian voting and his being independent on the reserve and enjoying his treaty rights. If we feel that the Indian has reached the point where he can safely vote, let us give him the vote regardless of whether he is a treaty Indian or not. Let there be no strings attached.
This was emphasized by the hon. member for Mackenzie, who gave a very fine talk on this matter. When the Indian becomes qualified for a job he should have a job to go to. In fact, I am beginning to think that we must adopt that attitude toward white people as well. When boys or girls are qualified for jobs I submit it is the duty of the government to see that they get jobs, even if it is necessary to create a new industry in order to provide such. I know that will be looked upon as rather extreme, but there is nothing more disheartening to a boy or girl coming out of *university than to be unable to get a job no matter where he or she may go to try. If the Indians are going to be given education and training, jobs must be waiting for them when they have completed that education and training. I cannot see any way of escaping that conclusion if we are going to create among the Indians a sound morale.
The same thing is true of the goods they produce, the fish, the lumber, the furs and wheat. It is one thing for white men to compete with each other for a share of the 'world's markets, but it is another thing altogether for the Indian to do that. He does not possess anything like the facilities with which to force his way into world markets that the white man has.
I think that will constitute the main portion of what I have to say. There are two other matters which I think need attention, one

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak on this subject at this time, but after listening to the well-prepared discourses we have heard this afternoon I feel that I have a story which I should tell in connection with the Indians in the territory which I am fortunate to represent. Incidentally, the reserve of these Indians is located within half a mile of my own home in the town of Enderby. We have heard in this debate calls for a royal commission, and we have heard details of the situation of the Indians in Saskatchewan and Alberta. We have heard the splendid plea by the hon. member for Lethbridge for the alleviation of distress among the Indians.
After listening to the details of the hardships suffered by many Indians I am beginning to think that the Indians in British Columbia are living in a pretty good part of the country. Of course I know that, and I have always preached that British Columbia is the garden of Eden. After listening to the details of the plight of the Indians in Saskatchewan and Alberta I am beginning to believe that is more and more the fact. I was surprised to hear that throughout the reserves in Saskatchewan there has been on an average one new house built per reserve during the past year. I have never gone through the reserve counting the houses, but I know that within two miles of Enderby there have been at least 25 houses built on the reserve during the past two years. They are scattered much farther afield than that. They are not just congregated in one place as a showpiece for the reserve. You can drive through the reserve and see the new houses.
As I listened to the pleas made for legislation and departmental action I wondered whether that was the answer. It appears to me that the problem is to find some way of integrating the Indian into the life of the local community. I do not mean to take the Indian off the reserve, I mean to make him acceptable to the community life of the white people in the areas adjacent to the reserve. I must admit that this is a local problem and its solution depends entirely upon the leaders in the white community who might be interested in the welfare of the Indian.
There is no doubt that the person best able to provide that leadership is the Indian

agent. I will go further and say that it is the responsibility of the department of Indian affairs to see that we have Indian agents able to give that leadership. I think we have perhaps not the only agent of that nature but certainly a young man with great vision.
I refer to Mr. Hett who is stationed at Vernon. He is certainly doing a mighty fine job in building up morale among the Indians of that area and getting the co-operation of the white community in assisting him in integrating the Indian into the life of the various communities.
Of course the place to start is with the young, and the Indians are no different than the white people in that respect. Sometimes old fellows-I am not excepting some of us in the house-are not amenable to change, but if we can get this across to the young generation it will be an easy matter to instil in them a different outlook and viewpoint.
For many generations we have looked upon the Indian as a second class citizen. I attach no blame for that feeling to either the Indian or the white man, but we must get rid of that stigma, if you want to call it that, and try to make the Indian a first class citizen. In my area we have no separate Indian schools. The Indian children attend the local public schools in Vernon, Enderby, Armstrong, Salmon Arm and I believe every place I could mention. They are not even in separate classrooms. They are free to mingle in their classes, in their sports and in their studies with the white children on a common ground and on a common basis.
It may be that there are many white people, who are not prepared to accept the Indians as an equal but in most cases, especially among children, you find no difference. We also find that the Indians have their bright students and their average students and some who are not even average, but the brighter students are certainly encouraged to go on to higher education, and we have them in the vocational schools and nurses' training schools, and we even have one or two students in the university. So a start has been made in that direction toward encouraging Indians to seek higher education.
We have had no trouble in placing educated Indians in employment. I will go further and say that we have found no trouble among the Indians in regard to earning a living in the local mills and in the woods and in the various jobs open to them in the white community. There is only one complaint I have. There is one large mill in my town that will not hire Indians, for the reason that they will work only two or three days or a week and then go away. For
Indian Act
that reason this particular man will not accept Indians, except possibly on a casual day to day labour basis. However, in the main we have Indians working in the mills and in the bush, earning a good deal of money on a scale equal to white people and building up very good homes for themselves on the reserves.
There is one other thing I should like to mention at this time. I spoke of the Indian agent giving leadership to the community or to the Indians on the reserve. Of course he cannot handle that by himself. The only way he can do that is by enlisting the support of people in the white community who are prepared to give some of their time and devote some effort to this work. I just want to tell you a little experience I had last summer. Mr Hett, the agent from Vernon, was anxious to get something started on the reserve, and a special meeting was called in our city hall. At that meeting we had the mounted police detachment-only two of them, by the way-I was at it, and also various other people of the community interested in trying to evolve some way to benefit and give a little lift to life on the reserve.
Of course at a meeting such as that there are always various ideas put forth, and at this one there were several. As a result we had some of the women and men from the town of Enderby who were prepared to devote one night a week or one night a month, as was required, to meet with the Indians and try to educate them into better ways of living. As a result we had a homemakers' club organized on the reserve. By the way, they have a very nice community hall less than half a mile from the limits of our city, and they meet there once a month. Different women from the town of Enderby attend these meetings and give hints and lessons on various phases of homemaking.
In a very short time results have been noticeable. When one drives along the roads through the reserve one sees that the washing on the line, for instance, is a little whiter than it used to be. One sees some brightly coloured curtains hanging at the windows, and one notices some painting and decorating being done on the houses. Inside the houses one will find action being taken in painting and decorating these homes. That is the result of the spirit that has been engendered in that community through the leadership of the people of Enderby.
We all know that sport is one of the greatest ways to level off the thinking of people. In that community we have Indians on the baseball clubs and on the hockey teams. Since I left there I have noted that a boxing

Indian Act
club has been organized in our little town. The corporal of the mounted police has offered his services to give lessons and supervise this club. I understand that among the membership are many Indian youths.
This is something that can be done by local effort; and you can build up the spirit that desires to see the Indian brought up to the standard or integrated into the white man's way of life. I think you can talk about legislation from now till doomsday but you cannot legislate these things for the Indians. They have to come through joint effort and through some encouragement from the white people. Leadership must come from the Indian agent and the white people of the communities surrounding the reserves. There are perhaps many other things I could mention, but my whole aim is to stress the point that I doubt very much whether legislation is the answer to this problem. That is the message I tried to convey to the meeting which, as I have said, was held last fall. It is up to us to remove that feeling of inferiority from the Indian and give him to understand that he will be accepted into the circles of the white man.
We have heard a little about drinking. In our province the Indians are allowed into the beer parlours. They get tight on occasion. I doubt if they get any tighter or act any worse than some of our white men. At the same time, I have not been too happy about legislation giving the Indians the right to enter beer parlours and to have liquor freely. The problem in giving liquor to Indians is that it is just one more means by which they get rid of their money, which is not too plentiful.
Many are heads of families. I happen to know quite well a family with 14 children. They have a new house, but I will grant you that it is not big enough for 14 children. The head of this household is working and makes from $10 to $12 per day. All the children of school age are attending school. They are very well dressed, too. However, with $10 or $12 per day the wife finds it difficult to provide school lunches and properly look after these 14 children, of whom I think ten are of school age. That is a problem that would be just as much a problem for a white person. However, I must say that, of the Indians of whom I have knowledge or acquaintance, they seem to be making progress in what I think is the proper way.
I would again emphasize what has been done in this area where leadership has come from the Indian agent, and it seems to be the only one we have heard about. I would say it is up to the Indian affairs branch to see that we have more of this type of Indian

agent. That is where the responsibility of the department lies. I think that is something that should be studied and considered. I have no doubt that it is being given consideration, and that possibly the officials of the department know a whole lot more about what is being done in Vernon and my area generally than I do. However, this is something that should be publicized for it does show, rather than through legislation or reserve improvement, one way in which the Indian can be made part of the community life and accepted on a par with the white man of this country.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Pickersgill thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 439, to amend the Indian Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION, MAKE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the resolution indicates, this bill is designed to extend the application of certain provisions of the act to certain persons or groups of persons who are not at present able to benefit from it. These extensions in turn call for certain consequential amendments, and in addition the bill will deal with other amendments of an administrative nature.
The principal amendment proposed has to do with the making of an election to continue as a participant after retirement under part II of the act, which provides the supplementary death benefits. It is proposed to provide a year in advance of retirement in which an election may be made in addition to the present very limited period of 3 days following retirement. A provision is also proposed which would validate elections which could not be accepted in the past since they were made just prior to retirement. Many hon. members are aware of this problem, which is a rather complicated one, and I would suggest that any detailed discussion

should be deferred until there has been an opportunity to study the amending bill.
Another major amendment proposed would repeal those provisions in the act which would have come into force on August 1, 1957, and which would have restricted the augmenting of pension credits through employment after the age of 65 on and after that date.
The other amendments proposed will, I think, commend themselves to the house as relatively minor in nature and, as I mentioned previously, relate primarily to the elimination of administrative problems. The most important of these would require that re-employed former contributors under the act on again becoming contributors would be treated like all new employees and would become participants under the supplementary death benefit scheme under part II of the act, regardless of the fact that they had elected not to participate when the death benefit scheme was introduced in the house a year or two ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION, MAKE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that there should be general approval of the purpose expressed in regard to the amendments mentioned in the statement just given to the committee. However, I would strongly urge that the opportunity be taken to deal with a subject which goes much farther than the amendments now proposed and involves an improvement that I think is greatly needed in connection with the Public Service Superannuation Act. I mention that because while we are in the committee stage we are simply dealing with the desirability of introducing a measure to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act and to extend its application. For that reason it would be possible to redraft the bill, if it is in final drafted form, to include any suggestions that may be made. So it is appropriate on a motion of this kind to indicate the nature of amendments not already mentioned but which, in the opinion of many hon. members, could and should be included.
In the statement just made it has been indicated that the legislation is designed to extend the application of the present act to certain people to whom it does not now apply. It is also intended to provide a wider opportunity for election under the act. It seems that the remainder of the amendments are largely for the purpose of facilitating administration.
I believe the time is long overdue in Canada for an amendment to the act which will recognize the severe hardship being suffered by many former civil servants, members of the armed forces, former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and others whose
Public Service Superannuation Act pensions were fixed at a time that the dollar was worth a great deal more than it is today. What I have to say does not of course apply to the disability pensions for service veterans, because consideration is given to them under another act.
I would point out, however, that it must be well known to all hon. members that there are men and women who gave long years of faithful service either in the civil service of Canada, as members of the armed forces, as members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or in the related services, whose pensions today, with the present value of the dollar, are hopelessly inadequate to meet the minimum demands of decent living. When this subject has been discussed on other occasions there has been some tendency to suggest that the amount paid was in the nature of a contract. There is the suggestion that it would be a practical impossibility to review the whole field of pension payments in these categories. I suggest, however, that we should consider the reasons for which these pensions were established.
It is recognized that those in the civil service, in the armed forces, in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and in other similar services are not paid as much as people of similar skill, devotion to their task and general ability might earn in private occupations. The pension has been regarded as something that will make it possible for them to live in modest decency in the years of their retirement after the active period of their service. Actually the date of retirement may be a fairly early one. For that reason we must consider this matter as an obligation of justice. Their pensions were fixed at a time when doubtless, in many cases, they were adequate to meet the demands of the principle upon which they had been established. It seems to me that this is a question of justice to those who have served their country well. In making the suggestion that there should be a review and that there should be amendments to the superannuation act at this time, I am not making any suggestion that is impractical or that is in any way beyond the ordinary considerations of government.
I would point out that similar consideration has been given to this problem in both the United Kingdom and the United States. To take the United Kingdom, where the parliamentary system is similar to our own and where the form of service may be more similar, I would point out that there have been a number of acts increasing the pensions payable to people in the categories I have mentioned as well as to others.
5580	HOUSE OF
Public Service Superannuation Act As evidence of this I merely give the fact that in 1920 an act was rpassed known as the Pensions (Increase) Act, 1920. Again there was the Pensions (Increase) Act of 1924. Then there was the Pensions (Increase) Act of 1944. Later there was the Pensions (Increase) Act of 1947. Later still there was the Pensions (Increase) Act of 1956, which came into effect on April 1 this year. In the Pensions (Increase) Act of 1956 the increase of pension embraced 20 different categories. It would perhaps naturally embrace a wider number of categories in the United Kingdom than it would here in any event, because of the fact that with a single government there, a number of services that would fall under the provincial governments in this country fall under the central government there.
The amounts of the increases have varied. This year they have varied in accordance with the amount of the pension payable, and it is not a rigid pattern. At the time this bill was before the House of Commons in the United Kingdom I find the statement of the financial secretary to the treasury, Mr. Henry Brooke, as reported at page 585 of British Hansard for February 23 of this year. During the course of those remarks he had this to say:
What we have to do is to take into account a total body of about 600,000 pensioners, who have retired after different kinds of services, with different kinds of pension, at different times over the past 30 years and more. What matters is to do justice, as far as possible, among all those individuals. One has to discard the idea of a simple, new scheme as soon as one discovers that whatever scheme of that kind one can devise, it will do justice that is too rough to be called justice at all.
Mr. Brooks then went on to explain the system that was being adopted, and later in the same day he explained:
The fact is that the earlier acts have given a much greater percentage increase the smaller the pension.
That practice has generally been followed. Nevertheless there has been a general review in the United Kingdom of the whole problem of pensions fixed years ago, at a time when the value of money was a great deal more than it is today in terms of the same units. That bill passed this year was one of a long series, as I have indicated. It shows that it is an accepted part of their practice in the United Kingdom to attempt to deal with this subject on the basis of justice which relates to the duty to give to those who have served the country in various capacities a minimum decent living standard in keeping with their place in the community.


I would point out that this principle has been accepted by three different parties in Britain. It was accepted by the Conservative government which passed the act this year; by the coalition government in 1944; by a Labour government since then; and in earlier years by a Liberal government. Therefore in the United Kingdom no argument is presented that any cold, contractual basis should limit the amount payable to those elderly citizens who have given fine service to the country and whose pensions were intended to give them a minimum decent standard of living.

speechtext:
At six o'clock I was speaking on the efforts that have been made in the United Kingdom to deal with the problem of pensions to civil servants, to members of the armed forces and others on the basis of the changing value of money, and I had given references to the acts which had been passed there to deal with that tremendously important problem. I did so merely to indicate that this is not a theoretical suggestion in any way, and I proposed that the act here be amended to take care of the situation with which we are confronted in this country.
I would like also to point out that in the United States which it is true has a different form of government, they have dealt with this same problem and on different occasions have made changes to bring the pensions in some way into balance with the changing value of money. In doing so they have recognized that this is not something which can be regarded merely as a contract for a fixed amount of money, but that what we have in mind is a decent living standard for people who have served their country in one public capacity or another. In 1930 they passed an act which provided for an increase of annuities and again, in 1955, they made certain changes in the earlier statute. I quote from page 4750 of what is described as the

United States code, congressional and administrative news, which covers the laws passed in the United States during 1955. I see that at page 4750 it says:
As will be seen from the schedule, the formula favours the low-annuity individual who most needs the increase.
Nevertheless, I find that in the United States laws, as well as in the laws passed in the United Kingdom, an attempt has been made to examine the whole situation and find, on the basis of justice, what would be a fair, decent and reasonable minimum standard for those who are dependent upon the pensions paid in this way.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that when we find in the United Kingdom, which is under a similar system to our own, and in the United States, which is under a different system but which is so close to us geographically that they have dealt with this subject in the way they have, we should be prepared to deal with it here. I think it must be known to many hon. members that there are many people, who gave long years of devoted service, who are living in the most severely restricted conditions today and in fact are living in conditions that we should not feel to be satisfactory for those who have given long years of public service. I do think that in the amendments now proposed some steps should be taken to deal with this subject. I believe that as a first step a uniform percentage increase should be agreed upon. However, I think it is essential that the whole subject be examined both in regard to the time at which the pensions were granted and the years of service that were given.
Even a uniform percentage would deal to some extent only with the problem with which we are confronted. Many of the people now with no other resources than the pensions of this kind which they receive had those pensions established at a time when the dollar was worth a great deal more than twice which it is worth today. Others received their pensions at a later date. It would seem that there are variable factors which must be taken into consideration.
I do not wish to leave the impression that I am in any way suggesting we should hand over the responsibility for examining things of this kind to bodies other than representative bodies of this parliament; but we all know that there are occasions when a royal commission, which can proceed without any problem of the period during which parliament is sitting or otherwise, can perform services which are extremely helpful. Those who sometimes speak in critical terms of royal commissions forget how many useful achievements there are which can be directly 67509-355
2, 1956	5581
Public Service Superannuation Act attributed to the recommendations of royal commissions in this country.
The same is true in the United Kingdom; the same is true in each of the nations of the commonwealth which has a similar parliamentary system. It would seem to me that in this case it is not only desirable and expedient that a measure to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act be introduced for the purposes mentioned earlier in the discussion today, but also that this amending bill make some immediate provision for the people who are in dire need at this time in the face of the very real measure of inflation which has taken place here and elsewhere.
Then I suggest that this whole problem be examined by a royal commission, which could sit without interruption and could examine the scale of pensions that were granted at different times and make recommendations to us as to the way in which this very real and very human problem could be dealt with.
The suggestion is sometimes made that we abdicate our responsibilities when a royal commission is appointed to inquire into matters of this kind. That certainly is not so. A royal commission can only make recommendations, nothing more. It is then for parliament to decide what will be done in regard to the recommendations made. In this case the advantages of a royal commission would be that it could start its sittings as soon as it had been appointed, and could continue to hear evidence and examine the various aspects of this problem and then be prepared to make an appropriate recommendation which could be given due consideration whenever the next session of this parliament or a succeeding parliament meets.
In any event, whatever course is adopted I do wish to emphasize this fact which I am sure is known to many hon. members. There are many devoted public servants of other years who are living under most unsatisfactory conditions today because the pensions which were established in those earlier days are so inadequate for their requirements now.
I have made these recommendations at a time when the bill is not finally before us. It is open to the government to reconsider the exact wording of the bill that will be brought forward following this resolution. In view of the fact that this has been dealt with on numerous occasions over succeeding years by the parliament of the United Kingdom, and in view of the fact that it has been dealt with under similar principles by the congress of the United States, where living conditions are in many ways similar to our own, I urge that justice be done to those senior members of our civil service, our armed forces, our Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other

Public Service Superannuation Act similar servants so we may have the feeling that those who serve Canada well are at least receiving justice in this way.
May I suggest, without any thought other than the fact that the problem of maintaining the strength of this or any other country depends so much upon the civil service and the other services I have mentioned, that perhaps this is the day when we might most appropriately consider our responsibility to those who can only look to us for the measure of justice to which they are entitled.

In the first place I want to associate myself with the Leader of the Opposition in paying tribute to the quality of the civil service generally. I think the Minister of Finance particularly must be constantly aware of the problem of securing and retaining in the public service the best available people in the country in view of the tremendous competition offered by private enterprise.
I have before me a sessional paper which gives the names of the lawyers who have been employed by government departments and the legal fees and expenses paid to them. This return runs to over 100 pages, and I cannot but contrast the fees paid to a very few lawyers across the country with the salaries we pay to the lawyers who are in the cabinet or who serve with various government departments. I am sure the Minister of Finance himself finds it embarrassing at times to be negotiating with some of the top people in the Canadian financial world and to have to admit that the Minister of Finance receives an amount which is very small compared with the returns offered by the large financial corporations in this country.
I realize I cannot go too far in pressing this. Last year when the superintendent of insurance had performed an outstanding piece of work I suggested that when increases were being considered he should be kept in mind for an increase. One of the daily papers

which circulates in my constituency drew attention to the salary he was receiving. Certainly it is not too easy to explain to farmers who are hard pressed why a farmer member should be advocating higher salaries for people who to them appear to be receiving fairly adequate salaries, but I think we should all agree that working in the public service of a country like Canada should rate high, and that those who are asked to make a career in various government departments should be given salaries while they are working and pensions when they are too old to work which will compare favourably with the returns which are available in other sectors of our economy.
I would like to stress particularly the point which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made again and again concerning the large number of civil servants who have been forced to retire on pensions which might have appeared adequate when they started with the civil service 30, 40 or 50 years ago but are quite inadequate today. I am not like some members of parliament who stay in plush Ottawa hotels when they come here; my returns do not allow that. On three different occasions I have had a room in the homes of retired civil servants. I think it would be a good thing if more members of parliament would place themselves in positions where they can observe retired civil servants living in the city of Ottawa.

speechtext:
I did not hear that. Would the hon. member stand up? I would appreciate having him say it so I can hear it.
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre discussed this question on April 16, 1953, he pointed out that of the 10,572 retired civil servants, 1,468 were on a pension of less than $60 a month and there were 312 on a pension of less than $20 a month. The figures for widows of civil servants, who numbered 5,123, showed that more than half or 2,766 were on a pension of less than $40 a month, and 942 were on a pension of less than $20 a month.
There is a new Minister of Finance since the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre discussed this question; Mr. Abbott was the minister at that time. I am sure the present Minister of Finance will want to give careful consideration to the representations I am making before the bill is finally presented.
I notice that when Bill No. 334 was before the banking and commerce committee in April of 1953, Mr. Whitehouse, president of the Civil Service Federation of Canada, was called as a witness. In answer to a question

as to what other countries had done about the position of retired civil servants who were caught by inflation he was able to advise the committee that in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, the United States and some parts of Canada something had been done. Later, upon being questioned, he admitted that Saskatchewan was the one part of Canada where some provision had been made so that retired civil servants who found themselves with pensions of $40 or $60 a month would be put in a better position.
I submit that this is a domestic problem that the Minister of Finance and his experts can solve without any serious repercussions on our economy. It is very annoying for this large group of our retired civil servants to read articles in newspapers such as the one which appeared in the Toronto Telegram on June 27 of this year. This is a story written by Arnold Agnew from Ottawa and it is headed: "3 Months' Profits Hit $728,000,000- See Huge Surplus". The articles reads:
Corporation profits soared to an estimated $728 million in the first three months of this year, an increase of 28 per cent over the same period last year, dominion bureau of statistics figures show.
The increase in profits before taxes amounts to $158 million. Income tax liabilities for the first quarter were estimated at $321 million, an increase of 23 per cent over last year.
The figures bolster predictions that the dominion treasury will find itself with a huge surplus at the end of the year.
Then the last dominion bureau of statistics weekly bulletin had this to say about the gross national product:
Canada's gross national product rose during the first quarter of 1956 to a level equal to an annual rate of $28-3 billion, about 6 per cent above the annual average for last year and nearly 11-7 per cent above last year's first-quarter level. The quarter's rise reflected mainly a further rise in the physical volume of production. The output gain was concentrated in mining, forestry, construction, transportation and other service groups; manufacturing was little changed from the last 1955 quarter.
If the gross national product can go up 11-7 per cent in the first quarter of this year as compared with last year, and if corporation profits can go up 28 per cent for the first quarter of this year as compared with the first quarter of last year, I see no reason why the Minister of Finance cannot before proceeding with this legislation review the matter and bring in the necessary provision so that the large number of civil servants who retired on the assumption that the bond of the government of Canada was as good as gold and that the cheque they would receive in the evening of their lives would be adequate, should have further consideration.
On April 16, 1953, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when discussing this 67509-3551

Public Service Superannuation Act matter pointed out what had been done in the United States in 1948, when an act of congress was passed which increased the pensions of retired employees by 25 per cent or $300 a year, whichever was the lesser figure. If the United States in 1948 could provide either an increase of 25 per cent or $300 a year, whichever was the lesser, I am sure we could do the same thing in 1956. In 1952 a further increase was granted by another act of congress. As an example of how those two pieces of legislation worked out, a superannuant who was receiving $1,000 per year was increased in 1948 to $1,250 and in 1952 to $1,565.50. I think the same thing is physically possible on the Canadian scene.
I might mention in passing that apparently it is not too wise a political move for any member of parliament to cast reflections upon these most reasonable representations. I notice that one of the few members who was critical was the former member for Regina, Dr. McCusker. It is significant that he did not come back to Ottawa after the election. Of course there were other factors involved, but I think the fact that he was not able to make out a good case when this bill was before the house indicated that it would have been better for him if he had kept quiet.
Some time ago the Department of Labour produced an interesting study having to do with older workers. I think at this stage the minister should be prepared to give consideration to the large number of people who have retired but who are unable to have that standard of living which the economy of Canada could provide for all its citizens. The statistical branch of the Bank of Canada has presented some alarming information with regard to consumer credit in Canada. Since the beginning of 1951 when these figures were first compiled up to the end of 1955 the increase has been most alarming.
It is only natural that in the Canadian economy when there is such a wide variety of goods in our stores and when there are such a large number of people who are not getting salaries or pensions large enough to buy those goods, many would be encouraged to go into debt. We certainly are not going to be able to solve the economic problems of Canada by encouraging our pensioners or those who are not on pensions to go in debt to the storekeeper, to the finance company or to the bank in order to get consumer goods.
I find that in the United States there is a great deal of concern about this same trend. Large numbers of people are unable to pay

speechtext:
I think it would be more desirable to have the bill in our hands before we make too extended remarks about it. However, I should like to add a word to the comments which have been placed before the committee by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Mackenzie.
It is only parliament which in the final analysis can provide a just measure of security for our civil service both by way of salary and superannuation. As has been said, they look to us, and I think it is essential that we give the most earnest consideration to the position in which civil servants find themselves and do what we can, not only to attract the best possible men and women to the service but to see to it that the level of their salaries and superannuation is such as will give them the measure of security to which they are entitled.
I have been somewhat critical of some of the competitions which have been advertised and notices of which we find so frequently in our mail boxes. In my judgment the salary schedule is ridiculously low in
IMr. Nicholson.]

many cases when one considers the qualifications and experience required before a person can qualify for the position.
There was a time when it could be said that it was desirable to get a fat civil service job, but I am afraid now there are very few such, except perhaps at the top, and even then they are not too fat. I am afraid that we are not competing successfully with private industry. I think we are going to lose such people to private industry, and unless we become much more realistic about both salary schedules and superannuation arrangements we shall find ourselves very largely with second rate people in the civil service.
Now I should like to say just a word about the matter raised by the hon. member for Mackenzie, about the retired civil servant who found himself ten or 15 years ago on what was then considered a fairly good level of superannuation, one which he thought would provide him with some security for the rest of his life. Since then the value of the Canadian dollar has been allowed to decline seriously until its value is little more than 50 per cent of what it was in 1939. As a consequence the superannuant finds himself in the position that he has not half enough to take care of his needs during his declining years.
Now he is in a desperate position. It was not his fault that the dollar lost its purchasing value. He therefore can say, "I looked ahead; I did the very best I could to provide myself with security for my old age. I put up dollars that would purchase a dollar's worth, but I got back dollars that will purchase only 50 cents worth. Consequently I have to look somewhere for justice. I have to do something to supplement this meagre income; otherwise I simply cannot live." Many of them cannot find work. They are told they are too old to work.
May I point out there are two sides to this whole question. There is the humanitarian side. We owe it to those old civil servants, who gave the best years of their lives to the public service, to see to it that the dollars they get back under their superannuation schemes are equal in purchasing value to the dollars they put in. I think that is only right. That is the humanitarian side, because they need the security they have purchased. It is not their fault that they are not getting it. Somebody else has fallen down; the managers of our system and of our money policy.
There is another side to it, and that is the business side. From the point of view of stabilizing our economy it would be desirable to make provision for these retired civil

servants to have a better scale of pensions right now. It can be done; there is no question about it. I draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that last year we produced in this country $26,600 million worth of goods and services. In the course of producing that quantity of goods and services we distributed to the people of Canada over $24 billion worth of purchasing power in all forms. There was a deficiency, and that deficiency was made up very largely by the people of Canada running charge accounts, buying on instalment credit and borrowing from the banks or the personal loan companies and so on in the form of cash personal loans in order to satisfy their present needs and wants. We forced the people of Canada to borrow to the extent of $2,600 million last year in all those forms I mentioned, just in order that they could consume what they laboured so hard to produce.
That situation is more or less true each year. It would be a better stabilizer to our whole economy if the incomes of the people of Canada were more nearly equal to the value of the goods and services we produced, if we could see to it that purchasing power gets into their hands so they could buy what we produce without forcing them to go to the loan sharks to do it. We are forcing them to do that. Many of them are paying as much as 24 per cent a year to get the purchasing power with which to buy the goods and services that go begging for sale. That is not a good sign. That is not a stable, sound economy. I say that, entirely aside from the humanitarian aspect of this whole business, the Minister of Finance ought to see to it that these retired civil servants are given a better show for the dollars they put up to buy their superannuation. When he does, then our economy is going to be much more stable, we are going to bring our purchasing power more nearly into balance with our production, and our economy will be stronger and better for it.
So I suggest to the minister that what was said by the hon. member for Mackenzie is perfectly true. Canada can afford it. Canada cannot afford not to see that its old retired civil servants get a decent show. There is no reason in this world why they should continue to subsist on dollars that will buy only 50 cents' worth. I say it is high time that we in this parliament gave them justice; and only we can give them justice. I am going to leave it at that until the bill comes in.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on the Public Service Superannuation Act. As you know, Mr. 2, 1956
Public Service Superannuation Act Chairman, we in Canada have the most loyal and efficient public servants of any country in this world. We have been blessed by the fact that throughout the years, whatever government has been in power, we have had a wonderful staff of civil servants throughout the country. That places us in the position of having to deal with them fairly, equitably and most generously. I have always said that in any country the best employer should be the government, and I am proud to say that the government of Canada has the reputation of being the best employer in this country.
I have no quarrel with the superannuation act as it stands today; and no doubt unless conditions change gravely those who have been receiving pensions for the past few years and for many years to come will have an adequate superannuation. But my plea, as it has been for many years in the past, is for those who had already begun to receive pensions before 1950, and for those who receive small pensions in any case.
Dealing with those persons who received pensions before, say, 1950, it is true that many of those pensions are substantial. But in any event those pensions, as has been stated, do not provide the expected results for those who contributed for some 30 or 35 years before they were put on their pensions. I would say that even for these people a small percentage, at least, of increase should be allowed in any plan affecting pensions already in force.
But my real plea is for those who have low pensions. Low pensions arise for many reasons, one of the main reasons being the fact, that the people were on low salaries before-the war years, and pensions based on those low salaries are very low indeed in 1956. Many people are suffering real hardships because of those pensions. But there are other-people who are suffering and who will suffer -because of low pensions. They are the people.-who have had to retire on account of sickness after a few years in the civil service. They are the people whose positions are abolished through no fault of their own. There are also the people who, because of certain unfortunate conditions of life, have to retire before they have completed 35 years of service.
If the pensions of any in these groups are below what is enough to provide them with a normal existence, with the result that they become a charge on others in the community or have to live a very meagre existence, then I say it is the duty and responsibility of parliament to see that those who were our former employees receive some

Public Service Superannuation Act additional benefits. This is not something that can be settled without proper study. I think the whole matter should be studied by whatever authority the government chooses, but it should be a body of qualified people who have had experience.
All these conditions I have mentioned previously should be studied, the conditions of life of the people who have low pensions, the conditions of life of the people who have retired because of illness or because of the abolition of positions. These conditions should be studied so the government and parliament will be able to see to it that those who were formerly employees of this country do not suffer for the lack of suitable pensions.
The answer is always given that those not formerly civil servants who are depending on pension or investment plans do not receive bonuses, but the conditions are different. Any person who joins the public service must come under the pension plan. He has to contribute to the plan. The government is already a partner in the plan, and much more than an equal partner so far as contributions are concerned. In the past few years the government has contributed $125 million or more to subsidize the fund. We have accepted the principle that we are backing the fund. If we can accept that principle, Ahen I think we can also accept the principle that this time we are going to create a fund once and for all to support those who have *been let down by the changes in salaries and ffhe new plan of superannuation introduced 'some years ago.
I therefore urge that the Minister of Finance give this matter a great deal more attention than it has been given in the past. I think it is a matter of justice, a matter of fairness, a matter of equity, and it is also a question of being humanitarian. I hope the day will come when we can say there is nothing wrong with the conditions of employment of civil servants in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the discussion on the resolution stage preceding the introduction of a bill gives one the opportunity to make suggestions as to what should be included in the bill, and this evening I should like to deal with two points. In the first place, there is the question raised by the Leader of the Opposition, which has also been dealt with by spokesmen from each of the other parties.
I believe the time has come when the government should take some action. I remember it being raised first in the session of 1949, I think it was, and every year since that time the same thing has been pointed out to the government. However, we have

been brushed aside each year primarily with the argument that a contract had been made, that these civil servants knew what they were doing when they paid into the superannuation fund, and that the contract could not be changed now.
I submit that is not an answer to this problem. It has been found to be no answer in the United Kingdom, the United States, some of the Canadian provinces and in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway and many other private firms. I have here a letter from the superannuated federal civil servants organization of Vancouver written this year after checking the situation in other countries and with other organizations. They have this to say:
All countries that we have been able to contact have increased superannuation benefits to all those who were retired on the basis of pre-inflation salary rates, on humanitarian grounds. Two we might mention, namely, Great Britain and the United States, have given several increases to this class, and as recently as October 1, 1955, the United States have provided its fourth increase to the amount of 12 per cent to those receiving $150 per month or less and 8 per cent to those over $150.
I believe the organizations representing civil servants now in the service have urged from time to time that something be done to assist the superannuated civil servants, and surely the time has come to do something about it. Members of parliament have improved their own position on more than one occasion since this need was first pointed out, yet nothing has been done to help those retired civil servants. It really gets down to the basis of what it costs to live; and it costs a man who retired ten years ago, or his widow, just as much to live as it costs a civil servant retiring in 1956. I hope that in this bill or in other legislation the minister will make some provision to meet this situation.
The other point I should like to draw to the minister's attention has to do with the position of a widow who happens to be more than 20 years younger than her husband. Section 13, subsection 4, deals with that situation and reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, the amount of any annual allowance to which the widow of a contributor may be entitled under this act shall, if the age of the contributor exceeded that of his widow by 20 or more years, be reduced by an amount determined in accordance with the regulations.
I suggest that a provision of a little different type should be placed in the act to cover that situation. When a civil servant has been married for a period of 25 years, let us say, it does seem to me pretty severe treatment, when he dies and his widow happens to be over 20 years younger, that

her pension should be reduced. Surely the way to go at it would be to say that if he had been married for 10 years or 15 years, then the widow would receive the full amount payable to other widows. But this section is so worded that if the man happens to marry a woman over 20 years his junior she cannot qualify for the full widow's pension.
I suggest to the minister that is unfair and should be remedied. I have no doubt that there would be a comparatively small number of cases which would come under that provision, but I happen to have run across one where the widow, although she was over 20 years younger than the civil servant, was nearly 60 when he died and she has had her pension cut drastically as a result of that particular section. Apparently they did not realize that there was any such provision in the act, and kept on making payments expecting that in the event of his death the widow would get the same payment as any other widow. I hope the minister will look into that particular situation as well and that perhaps something can be done about it at this present session.
